explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. Job remembers God's lamp shining above his head, and he says he walked through the darkness by His light. I think that's a big part of what he misses. No flashlight on earth competes with that.

The moon is a fair guess, since it's the night light everybody knows. But Job never mentions it. He says he walked through the darkness by God's light, with His lamp shining above his head. Sorry, moon, you got left out of this one.
That's not the lamp Job names, friend. He says it was God's lamp that shone above his head, and he walked through the darkness by His light. I bet that made the dark feel a lot smaller.

Yes, the Almighty. Job says that back then the Almighty was still with him, and his children were around him. Notice that little word "still." I think Job is looking at the empty space where all of that used to be.
No priest in this verse, friend. Job doesn't name a go-between at all. He says the Almighty Himself was still with him, and his children were around him. That's a pretty close circle.

Good thinking, because Job does say God watched over him in verse 2. But in verse 5 the word is the Almighty. He says the Almighty was still with him, and his children were around him. A watchman stands at the wall, but Job is talking about God being right there with him.

True, baker. Job says "…my steps were bathed in cream and the rock poured out for me streams of oil!" (Job 29:6) That's a man walking through plenty. I've only ever been bathed in cookie crumbs, and I'm not complaining.

It's actually true, friend. Job says "…my steps were bathed in cream and the rock poured out for me streams of oil!" (Job 29:6) He's remembering a time when good things just flowed his way. Even the rock was pouring out oil for him.

Right, baker. Job says the young men saw him and withdrew (Job 29:8). That's how they responded when he went out to the city gate and took his seat in the public square. They stepped back and made room for him. In the same verse, the old men rose to their feet.
Bowing to the ground is a big move, but Job doesn't say it. He says the young men saw him and withdrew. They pulled back, and that's all the verse tells us.
Friend, Job says the opposite. He says the young men saw him and withdrew, and withdrawing means pulling back. I'd be the one running up for a hug, but that's just me.
Not quite, friend. Job says the old men rose to their feet. The text tells us they stood up, so this one is False. I think that says a lot about how they saw him.
False is right, baker. Job says the old men rose to their feet. The young men withdrew and the old men stood up. Between the two, the square was doing a lot of moving.

explanations.answer: He rescued the poor who cried out
explanations.explanation: That's the reason. Job says people called him blessed because he rescued the poor who cried out and the fatherless who had no helper. Notice what he names there. It's the people he rescued.

explanations.answer: He owned the finest house in town
explanations.explanation: I understand the guess, but Job never mentions a house here. He says those who heard him called him blessed because he rescued the poor who cried out and the fatherless who had no helper. A house isn't in that verse.

explanations.answer: He won every battle he fought
explanations.explanation: No battles in this verse, friend. Job says people called him blessed because he rescued the poor who cried out and the fatherless who had no helper. It's about who he helped. A trophy shelf isn't mentioned anywhere.
It's the other way around, friend. Job says the dying man blessed him. He also says he made the widow's heart sing for joy. I think that's one of the sweetest things a man can say about his life.
False is right. Job says the dying man blessed him, and he made the widow's heart sing for joy. Those are the people he's remembering. I think it's a tender thing to recall.

Clothed is the word. Job says, "I put on righteousness, and it clothed me; justice was my robe and my turban." (Job 29:14) I wear an apron and a tall chef's hat, and he wore righteousness and justice. His outfit wins.

Followed sounds nice, but Job picks a different word. He says, "I put on righteousness, and it clothed me; justice was my robe and my turban." (Job 29:14) It's something he put on, from robe to turban. Righteousness wasn't tagging along behind him, it was what he wore.

Guarded makes sense for something so strong, friend. But the verse says, "I put on righteousness, and it clothed me; justice was my robe and my turban." (Job 29:14) He's describing clothing, from his robe to his turban. Righteousness covered him, head to toe.
Feet, yes. Job says he served as eyes to the blind and as feet to the lame. Those are his words for how he served them. That's a man you want at your side.
Hands is a good guess, and trust me, I know the value of good hands. Mine are a mustache. But Job says he served as feet to the lame, right after saying he was eyes to the blind.
Ears fit a man people came to for counsel. But for the lame, Job says he served as feet. Right before that, he says he was eyes to the blind.

explanations.answer: A long life ending in his own nest
explanations.explanation: That's what he pictured. Job says, "I will die in my nest and multiply my days as the sand." (Job 29:18) He thought he'd have a long life and end it at home. I think that's a picture of a man who felt settled.

explanations.answer: A short life ending far from home
explanations.explanation: That's the opposite of what Job thought. He says, "I will die in my nest and multiply my days as the sand." (Job 29:18) He expected a long life and an ending at home. A short life far away wasn't in his plans.

explanations.answer: A quiet life ending in a stranger's house
explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. Job says, "I will die in my nest and multiply my days as the sand." (Job 29:18) He pictured a long life, and he pictured it ending in his own nest. No stranger's house in the picture.

True. Job says, "My roots will spread out to the waters, and the dew will rest nightly on my branches." (Job 29:19) That's a tree with water at its roots and dew every night. I think he pictured a life that would keep growing.

It's actually true, friend. Job says, "My roots will spread out to the waters, and the dew will rest nightly on my branches." (Job 29:19) He pictured himself like a well-watered tree. The roots reach the water, and the dew settles on the branches every night.

Rain is right. Job says, "They waited for me as for rain and drank in my words like spring showers." (Job 29:23) Waiting for rain is waiting for something you really need. That's how much his words meant to them.

Sunrise is a pretty guess, but Job never uses it. He says, "They waited for me as for rain and drank in my words like spring showers." (Job 29:23) He's saying they wanted what he had to say, and they soaked it up.

Harvest is a good guess, friend, since people do wait for it. But Job picks something else. He says, "They waited for me as for rain and drank in my words like spring showers." (Job 29:23) It's all water here, from the rain to the showers.

King it is. Job says, "So I dwelt as a king among his troops, as a comforter of the mourners." (Job 29:25) And look at how he finishes that line. Right after the king comparison, he says he dwelt as a comforter of the mourners.

Prophet isn't the word he uses, friend. Job says he dwelt as a king among his troops, and as a comforter of the mourners. He says he chose their course and presided as chief. That sounds like a leader people followed.

Good thinking, because Job spent plenty of time helping people. But in this line, he says he dwelt as a king among his troops. Then he adds that he was a comforter of the mourners. It's a mix of a leader and a comforter, and both are in the verse.

Sheep dogs, yes. Job says he would have refused to put the fathers of these younger men with his sheep dogs. Those are strong words, and they show how far apart he sees them from himself. The text just gives us his words, so I'll let them stand.
Camels are a fair guess, but Job names another animal. He says he would have refused to put their fathers with his sheep dogs. Those are his words, not mine.

Oxen are strong animals, but Job doesn't name them here. He says he would have refused to put the fathers of the younger men with his sheep dogs. That's the animal in the verse. Dogs ended up with the spotlight.
True. Job says they abhor him and keep far from him, and they do not hesitate to spit in his face. I think this one hurts. It's a heavy part of what he's saying.

I wish it were false, friend, but Job says it plainly. He says they abhor him and keep far from him, and they do not hesitate to spit in his face. I think this one hurts. It's a heavy part of what he's saying.

That's what Job says. He says, "…God has unstrung my bow and afflicted me…" (Job 30:11) and that the men have cast off restraint around him. Earlier he spoke of his bow being renewed in his hand, and now he describes it unstrung. A bow without a string can't shoot.

Job doesn't mention thieves, friend. He says, "…God has unstrung my bow and afflicted me…" (Job 30:11) and he names God as the one who unstrung it. He describes the bow as unstrung. That's a big change from the way he spoke of it before.

Snapped makes it sound like an accident, but Job says something different. He says, "…God has unstrung my bow and afflicted me…" (Job 30:11) and he says it was God who did it. The bow is unstrung, which means it can't be used. In the good days he thought it would be renewed in his hand, and now he describes it this way.

His dignity. Job says terrors are turned loose against him, and they drive away his dignity as by the wind. That's something you can't pack up and carry home. He adds that his prosperity has passed like a cloud.

I see why you'd say friends, since Job talks a lot about people pulling away. But in this verse, Job says the terrors drive away his dignity as by the wind. He also says his prosperity has passed like a cloud. Friends aren't named there.

Servants are a fair guess, but Job doesn't name them here. He says terrors are turned loose against him, and they drive away his dignity as by the wind. His prosperity, he says, has passed like a cloud.

I wish that were true, friend. But Job says, "Night pierces my bones, and my gnawing pains never rest." (Job 30:17) The pains don't rest at night. This is a heavy line, and I think it's best to sit with it a second.
False is right. Job says, "Night pierces my bones, and my gnawing pains never rest." (Job 30:17) Night doesn't give him any relief. This is a heavy part of the passage.

True. Job says, "He throws me into the mud, and I have become like dust and ashes." (Job 30:19) Notice the word "like." He's describing how low he feels he's been put. I think that's a hard thing to say out loud.
It's true, friend. Job says, "He throws me into the mud, and I have become like dust and ashes." (Job 30:19) That's how he describes where he ends up. Heavy words, and they're his.

That's what Job says to Him. He says, "I cry out to You for help, but You do not answer; when I stand up, You merely look at me." (Job 30:20) These are Job's words, spoken straight to God. I think it's honest, and it's heavy.

That isn't in the verse, friend. Job says, "I cry out to You for help, but You do not answer; when I stand up, You merely look at me." (Job 30:20) He's talking right to God here. No messenger shows up in this line.

The verse doesn't say that. Job says, "I cry out to You for help, but You do not answer; when I stand up, You merely look at me." (Job 30:20) These are Job's words, spoken to God. He doesn't mention being told to wait.

He wept for them. Job asks, "Have I not wept for those in trouble? Has my soul not grieved for the needy?" (Job 30:25) He's pointing back at how he treated people in need. It matches what he said earlier, that he rescued the poor who cried out.

That's not what Job says. He asks, "Have I not wept for those in trouble? Has my soul not grieved for the needy?" (Job 30:25) He describes weeping and grieving for people in need. Staying away isn't the picture.

Job doesn't say that, friend. He asks, "Have I not wept for those in trouble? Has my soul not grieved for the needy?" (Job 30:25) Weeping and grieving is how he describes it. There's no blame in those words.
Help. Job says, "I stand up in the assembly and cry for help." (Job 30:28) Back then he was the one who rescued the poor who cried out. Now Job is the one crying out.

Revenge isn't the word, friend. Job says, "I stand up in the assembly and cry for help." (Job 30:28) He's calling for help in front of everyone. In the good days, he was the one answering those cries.

Silence is interesting, because in the good days people waited silently for his counsel. But in this verse, Job says, "I stand up in the assembly and cry for help." (Job 30:28) He isn't asking for quiet. He's asking for help, out loud and in public.
True. Job says, "My skin grows black and peels, and my bones burn with fever." (Job 30:30) He's describing what's happening to his body. It's a heavy line, so I'll let it be.

I wish it were false, friend, but Job says it right there. He says, "My skin grows black and peels, and my bones burn with fever." (Job 30:30) He's describing what's happening to his body. It's a heavy line.
Mourning. Job says, "My harp is tuned to mourning and my flute to the sound of weeping." (Job 30:31) His harp and his flute are tuned to grief. I think it's a sad note to end a speech on.

Praise is a lovely word, but it isn't what Job says here. He says, "My harp is tuned to mourning and my flute to the sound of weeping." (Job 30:31) The music he's describing is grief. It's a heavy way to end.

Victory is a hopeful guess, friend, but Job doesn't say that. He says, "My harp is tuned to mourning and my flute to the sound of weeping." (Job 30:31) The music he describes is mourning and weeping. That's how this speech ends.
